draft.title: Abstract nouns
card: names something you can see, touch, hear, taste or smell, such as bridge, dog or rain.
names an idea, quality or feeling that you cannot sense directly, such as courage, justice or grief.
Abstract nouns let a writer sum up a whole situation in one word. Instead of describing many unfair events, a writer can just write injustice.
Example: The town faced years of hardship. One word, hardship, covers lost jobs, empty shops and worry.
draft.remember: An abstract noun names an idea and can sum up a whole situation in one word.

a.q: Which word in this sentence is an abstract noun? The old fisher showed great patience at the pier.
a.why: Patience is a quality, and you cannot touch it. Fisher and pier are concrete nouns you can see. Old describes the fisher, so it is an adjective, not a noun.
a.clue: Which word names a quality you cannot touch?

b.q: A writer describes a village where many families were forced to leave their homes. Which abstract noun best sums up the situation in one word?
b.why: Displacement names the idea of people being forced from their homes, so it sums up the whole situation. Suitcase and village are concrete nouns. Moving is a verb form, so it is not an abstract noun that names an idea.
b.clue: Look for the word that names an idea, not an object.

problems.detail: Why (b) says 'Moving' is a verb form, so it is not an abstract noun. As a gerund ('moving' in 'the moving was hard') it works as a noun and can name an action or idea. The real reason it is weaker is that it does not capture being forced to leave, so the explanation should say that instead.

The right option, Displacement, is clearly the longest. It is also the only one with a typical abstract-noun suffix, while the distractors are two obvious concrete nouns and a verb form. A student could pick it without understanding the idea.
